J. |date=April 26, 2013 |title=Nick Saban |url=http://www.encyclopediaofalabama.org/article/h-3443 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221209034426/http://www.encyclopediaofalabama.org/article/h-3443 |archive-date=December 9, 2022 |access-date=December 24, 2022 |website=Encyclopedia of Alabama}} is an American [[sportscaster]] and former [[American football|football]] coach. He serves as an analyst for [[ESPN]]'s ''[[College GameDay (football TV program)|College GameDay]]'', a television program covering [[college football]]. He is widely considered to be one of the greatest football coaches of all time.{{Cite web |last=Dodd |first=Dennis |date=January 5, 2018 |title=The debate is truly over: Why Nick Saban is the greatest coach of all time |url=https://www.cbssports.com/college-football/news/the-debate-is-truly-over-why-nick-saban-is-the-greatest-coach-of-all-time/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180712052131/https://www.cbssports.com/college-football/news/the-debate-is-truly-over-why-nick-saban-is-the-greatest-coach-of-all-time/ |archive-date=July 12, 2018 |access-date=July 11, 2018 |website=CBSSports.com}}{{Cite web |last=Culpepper |first=Chuck |date=January 9, 2018 |title=Nick Saban is the top college football coach of all time |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/sports/colleges/nick-saban-is-the-top-college-football-coach-of-all-time/2018/01/09/bcf99eac-f56a-11e7-a9e3-ab18ce41436a_story.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180712040440/https://www.washingtonpost.com/sports/colleges/nick-saban-is-the-top-college-football-coach-of-all-time/2018/01/09/bcf99eac-f56a-11e7-a9e3-ab18ce41436a_story.html |archive-date=July 12, 2018 |access-date=July 11, 2018 |newspaper=The Washington Post}} Saban served as head coach of the [[National Football League]] (NFL)'s [[Miami Dolphins]] and at four universities: the [[University of Toledo]], [[Michigan State University]], [[Louisiana State University]] (LSU), and most famously the [[University of Alabama]], where he coached from [[2007 Alabama Crimson Tide football team|2007]] to [[2023 Alabama Crimson Tide football team|2023]] and led the team to six claimed [[College football national championships in NCAA Division I FBS|national championships]] and one unclaimed [[College football national championships in NCAA Division I FBS|championship]] in nine championship appearances during that period, as well as 9 [[Southeastern Conference|SEC]] titles and 10 SEC West Division championships. As a college football head coach, Saban won seven claimed national titles and one unclaimed national title, the most in college football history.{{Cite web |last=Staats |first=Wayne |date=January 12, 2021 |title=College football coaches with the most national championships |url=https://www.ncaa.com/news/football/article/2021-01-12/college-football-coaches-most-national-championships |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230312023511/https://www.ncaa.com/news/football/article/2021-01-12/college-football-coaches-most-national-championships |archive-date=March 12, 2023 |access-date=August 25, 2021 |website=NCAA.com}} His first came when he led the [[LSU Tigers football|LSU Tigers]] to the [[BCS National Championship Game|BCS National Championship]] in 2003. He then coached the [[Alabama Crimson Tide football|Alabama Crimson Tide]] to BCS and AP national championships in 2009, 2011, 2012, and to [[College Football Playoff]] championships in 2015, 2017 and 2020 with Alabama also having an unclaimed National Championship in 2016 that was selected by [[Colley Matrix|Colley]]. He became the first coach in college football history to win a [[College football national championships in NCAA Division I FBS|national championship]] with two different [[Football Bowl Subdivision]] (FBS) schools since the inception of the [[AP Poll]] in 1936.{{Cite web |last=Maisel |first=Ivan |author-link=Ivan Maisel |date=December 6, 2009 |title=Saban, Tide good for each other |url=https://www.espn.com/college-football/bowls09/columns/story?columnist=maisel_ivan&id=4796521 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100213092209/http://sports.espn.go.com/ncf/bowls09/columns/story?columnist=maisel_ivan&id=4796521 |archive-date=February 13, 2010 |access-date=April 1, 2010 |website=[[ESPN.com]]}} Saban and [[Bear Bryant]] are the only coaches to win an SEC championship at two different schools.{{Cite web |last=Kausler Jr. |first=Don |date=December 12, 2012 |title='The Process' will result in Nick Saban's 2013 induction into the Alabama Sports Hall of Fame |url=https://www.al.com/alabamafootball/2012/12/the_process_will_result_in_nic.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221224220635/https://www.al.com/alabamafootball/2012/12/the_process_will_result_in_nic.html |archive-date=December 24, 2022 |access-date=December 24, 2022 |website=[[The Birmingham News|AL.com]]}} Saban's career record as a college head coach is 292–71–1. 2025 |access-date=January 10, 2025 |publisher=Sports Illustrated}} {{TOC limit|3}} ==Early life and education== Saban was born in [[Fairmont, West Virginia]], to Mary and Nick Lou Saban Sr. and grew up in the nearby town of [[Monongah, West Virginia|Monongah]]. His parents owned a small service station and his father founded and coached a youth football team.{{Cite web |last=Hoge |first=Adam |date=January 6, 2013 |title=Hoge: Inside The Mind Of Nick Saban |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/chicago/news/hoge-inside-the-mind-of-nick-saban/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240218161748/https://www.cbsnews.com/chicago/news/hoge-inside-the-mind-of-nick-saban/ |archive-date=February 18, 2024 |access-date=February 18, 2024 |website=CBS News – Chicago |language=en-US}}{{Cite news |last=Bonesteel |first=Matt |date=January 11, 2024 |title=Nick Saban through the years: A timeline of his greatest hits |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/sports/2024/01/11/nick-saban-coaching-timeline-alabama-legacy/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://archive.today/20240111175530/https://www.washingtonpost.com/sports/2024/01/11/nick-saban-coaching-timeline-alabama-legacy/ |archive-date=January 11, 2024 |access-date=February 18, 2024 |newspaper=Washington Post |language=en}} He has one sister, Dianna, and graduated from Monongah High School in 1969.{{Cite web |last=Casagrande |first=Michael |date=June 21, 2016 |title=Newspaper scrapbook of Nick Saban's high school, college glory |url=http://www.al.com/alabamafootball/index.ssf/2016/06/nick_saban_scrapbook_of_high_s.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180802162541/https://www.al.com/alabamafootball/index.ssf/2016/06/nick_saban_scrapbook_of_high_s.html |archive-date=August 2, 2018 |access-date=December 24, 2022 |website=[[The Birmingham News|AL.com]]}}{{Cite web |last=Skipper |first=Clay |title=This Place Matters: The Tide Rolls Down from West Virginia |url=https://bittersoutherner.com/this-place-matters |access-date=September 26, 2024 |website=The Bitter Southerner |language=en-US}} In high school, Saban played [[high school football|football]]. He played quarterback and helped lead Monongah to the 1968 West Virginia Class A state championship his senior year.{{Cite web |last=Scarborough |first=Alex |date=November 14, 2018 |title=How Nick Saban's 1968 title explains the legendary coach |url=https://www.espn.com/college-football/story/_/id/25267700/nick-saban-first-championship-west-virginia-high-school |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221207003105/https://www.espn.com/college-football/story/_/id/25267700/nick-saban-first-championship-west-virginia-high-school |archive-date=December 7, 2022 |access-date=December 24, 2022 |website=[[ESPN.com]]}} Among his teammates were [[Kerry Marbury]], who went on to star for the [[West Virginia Mountaineers football|West Virginia Mountaineers]] and play in the [[Canadian Football League]].{{Cite web |last=Hrin |first=Eric |date=June 30, 2019 |title=Kerry Marbury gets final farewell |url=https://www.timeswv.com/news/kerry-marbury-gets-final-farewell/article_5aca3b68-9ade-11e9-8751-b7bd9d705834.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190709033610/https://www.timeswv.com/news/kerry-marbury-gets-final-farewell/article_5aca3b68-9ade-11e9-8751-b7bd9d705834.html |archive-date=July 9, 2019 |access-date=July 21, 2019 |website=Times West Virginian}} Saban attended [[Kent State University]] in [[Kent, Ohio]], and played defensive back for the [[Kent State Golden Flashes football|Golden Flashes]] under coach [[Don James (American football)|Don James]]. He and a roommate avoided being part of the [[Kent State shootings]], on May 4, 1970, when they decided to eat lunch before walking to the rally area.{{Cite web |date=May 5, 2008 |title=Saban remembers Kent State Shootings |url=http://www.sportsbybrooks.com/nick-saban-remembers-kent-state-shootings-17560 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090218194233/http://www.sportsbybrooks.com/nick-saban-remembers-kent-state-shootings-17560 |archive-date=February 18, 2009 |website=SPORTSbyBROOKS}} While attending KSU, he married Terry Constable, also from West Virginia, on December 18, 1971 in Fairmont.{{Cite web |last=Kelly |first=Nick |date=December 18, 2021 |title=On 50th anniversary, Nick Saban and Miss Terry share their love story |url=https://www.tuscaloosanews.com/story/sports/college/football/2021/12/18/nick-saban-wife-miss-terry-50th-wedding-anniversary-alabama-football/6468165001/ |access-date=2025-01-25 |website=Tuscaloosa News}} Saban graduated from Kent State in 1973 with a [[bachelor's degree]] in business, and in 1975, earned his [[master's degree]] in sports administration, also from Kent State. Saban's father died during his son's first year of [[graduate school]].{{Cite web |last=Grobeck |first=Joe |date=June 19, 2022 |title=Nick Saban's Dad's Early Death Inspires Him to be Great Every Single Day |url=https://fanbuzz.com/college-football/sec/alabama/nick-saban-dad/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221224221619/https://fanbuzz.com/college-football/sec/alabama/nick-saban-dad/ |archive-date=December 24, 2022 |access-date=December 24, 2022 |website=FanBuzz}} Saban is of [[Croats|Croatian]] ancestry.{{Cite web |last=Bach |first=Nenad N. |date=January 18, 2004 |title=(E) Croatian Nick Saban – Coach of the Year |url=http://www.croatia.org/crown/articles/7993/1/E-Croatian-Nick-Saban---Coach-of-the-Year.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221224221241/http://www.croatia.org/crown/articles/7993/1/E-Croatian-Nick-Saban---Coach-of-the-Year.html |archive-date=December 24, 2022 |access-date=December 24, 2022 |website=www.croatia.org}} His paternal grandfather, Stanko Saban, was born in 1895 in [[Gospić]], in the [[Lika]] region of [[Croatia]].{{cn|date=January 2026}} Stanko emigrated to [[Portland, Oregon]], in 1908, when he was 13 years old. He later married Anna Mihalic, of Croatian-American heritage.{{cn|date=January 2026}} ==Coaching career== ===Early coaching career=== Saban had not intended to enter the coaching ranks until [[Don James (American football)|Don James]] hired him as a graduate assistant at Kent State, while Saban waited for his wife to graduate.{{Cite web |last=Staples |first=Andy |date=August 14, 2012 |title=Sabanization of College Football |url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/2012/writers/andy_staples/08/14/sabanization-of-college-football/1.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120817015531/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/2012/writers/andy_staples/08/14/sabanization-of-college-football/1.html |archive-date=August 17, 2012 |access-date=January 11, 2012 |website=SI.com}} He later served as an assistant coach in [[NCAA Division I Football Bowl Subdivision|NCAA Division I-A]], at several schools: [[Syracuse Orange football|Syracuse]] in 1977, [[West Virginia Mountaineers football|West Virginia]] in [[1978 West Virginia Mountaineers football team|1978]] and [[1979 West Virginia Mountaineers football team|1979]],
